name: Creme
lede: Creme is a very pale lemon yellow, brighter than the cream of everyday speech, and it keeps a French spelling for a color the English call cream.

sections.title: The French spelling
sections.body:
In our library Creme is a name from the ISCC-NBS lists of 1955 and the xkcd survey of 2010, and its swatch is a pale lemon [3]. Its nearest everyday name is Cream, 6.0 units away, and it has a near-duplicate, Light Beige, that is only 0.3 units apart [3]. See [[cream]] for the plain English word.

Paterson defines cream as yellowish-white [1]. The swatch here is clearly more yellow and brighter than that, so the screen color is lemon cream, closer to custard than to milk [1][3]. Light Beige, its near-twin, shows how little separates a yellow-tinged cream from a pale beige on a screen [3].

sections.title: A cream that is violet
sections.body:
Paterson lists *crème de violette*, the violet liqueur, as a color term meaning a deep violet [1]. It sits in the violet group of his colour index [1]. See [[lavender]] and [[violet]] for the plain names.

Pastoureau's short book on color records another use [2]. In the courts of the 1600s and 1700s aristocrats smeared themselves with creams to make a white mask, and Pastoureau ties this to a wish to look unlike tanned peasants [2]. Those creams were cosmetics, not a color name, but they share the cream's association with pale skin [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Creme appears in 24 of our 23,781 paintings, about 0.1%, as photographed, and the within-painting lens finds it in 8 [3]. It is rarer than 70% of the named colors [3]. The earliest match is a work of 1599, and the 16 dated paintings at least 2% covered run to 1910 [3].

The name's earliest record in our sources is 1955, 356 years later, so a match is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not proof of a pigment [3]. In printed English the adjective peaks in the 2000s and rose fastest in the 1980s [3].
